title: One-to-one chat
brief: People send short messages to each other from their phones. A message must arrive once, in order, even when the phone is on a bad connection and sends it again. If the other person is offline, the message waits and a notification goes out.

clarify.q: What if the phone loses signal mid-send?
clarify.a: The app retries. The message must still arrive exactly once.

clarify.q: What if the other person is offline?
clarify.a: Save the message and send a push notification. They get it when they open the app.

clarify.q: Can a message ever be lost?
clarify.a: Never. Once the app shows one tick, the message is safe on your side.
Millions of phones wake up and reconnect in the same minute and ask what they missed.

notes: A delivery receipt ("delivered", "read") counts as an event.

numbers.label: Messages stored per day
numbers.how: about 40 per person per day x 10 million (approx.)

numbers.label: Storage added per year
numbers.how: 400 million x 1 KB x 365 = about 146 TB (approx.)

hints: What stops the same message from showing up twice when the phone retries?
Give every message an id made by the phone. An idempotency store remembers ids already seen, so a retry changes nothing.
Try: phones -> websocket gateway -> chat servers -> idempotency store, then a wide-column store for messages and a push service for offline people. Spread everything over three zones.

editorial.summary: The hard part of chat is not volume, it is "exactly once" on a bad network. The phone gives each message an id; the server checks a fast store of ids before saving. Messages go to a store built for huge appends. A held-open connection delivers to online people, and a push notification reaches the offline ones.

designs.name: Sockets, idempotency and a message log
designs.why: The websocket gateway holds the connections and delivers instantly to people online. Chat servers check the idempotency store, write to a wide-column store, and ask the push service to nudge offline recipients. Three zones keep it running when a building fails.

tradeoffs: Storing each message in three zones before saying "sent" costs a few milliseconds but means a failed building loses nothing.
The idempotency store adds one quick lookup per message. It is the price of "never twice".
Holding open connections costs memory on the gateways, but is far cheaper than phones asking "any news?" every few seconds.
A morning reconnect surge can be absorbed with spare gateway capacity, or spread out by having phones wait a random moment before reconnecting.
editorial.realWorld: A single well-built chat server can hold several hundred thousand open connections (approx.). Large messaging apps handle tens of billions of messages a day, mostly small and mostly delivered within a second.

correctness.prompt: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.
